paras: The threatened lynching of John Wilson took place in Valparaiso, Indiana, on the night of August 8, 1903, when crowds of angry farmers gathered near the Porter County jail and talked of lynching Wilson, a Black man jailed that evening on a charge of attacking a farmer's wife. The sheriff doubled the guard, no attack was made, and Wilson was later sentenced to two to fourteen years in prison. The episode drew wider notice after a Chesterton editor, A. J. Bowser, cited it in starting a campaign against Black settlement in Porter County.

According to the Indianapolis Journal's Valparaiso correspondent, a stranger came to the Washington township farm home of Mrs. U. S. Biggs on the afternoon of August 8 asking for matches, then returned. He was accused of choking and kicking her in an attempted "criminal assault" until her children's cries drove him off; physicians later reported a broken collarbone and three broken ribs. The Journal tied the strength of local feeling partly to an earlier attack on a young woman at a Valparaiso cemetery.

A posse of nearly 100 armed farmers chased the man, who boarded a freight train and was captured at Wanatah by Deputy Sheriff Matthews and Billy Wilson, a schoolteacher, who felled him with a stone when he drew a knife. Jailed in Valparaiso that evening, he gave his name as John Wilson of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania.

Within an hour, the Plymouth Tribune reported, the streets were crowded with farmers "bent upon dealing summary punishment." Farmers bought cartridges and a businessman offered rope, but, in the Journal's words, "lack of a leader" prevented an attempt on the jail. Sheriff La Count doubled the jail force, and by midnight the streets were quiet. The Journal said Wilson admitted assault and battery but denied rape; the wire report said he had confessed.

On Sunday the correspondent saw no further attempt to form a mob, though neighbors said the posse would have "made quick work" of Wilson, and pastors urged that the law take its course. Armed guards stayed at the jail, and on the night of August 10 armed farmers waited along the road on a rumor that Wilson would be moved.

By August 11 a number of Black residents had left for Chicago and two Black businessmen were "practically forced to suspend." Bowser then organized opposition to Black settlement, writing that it would expose white women to "a fate more horrible than death" and that "lynchings would follow," and later urged residents to refuse to rent, sell or give work to Black newcomers.

Fearing the continuing feeling, officials held Wilson's preliminary hearing secretly on August 22; he pleaded not guilty and was bound over. On October 6 Judge Tuthill sentenced him to two to fourteen years at Michigan City, after Wilson argued that another man had committed the act.

All located coverage came from white papers, led by the Indianapolis Journal, which followed the case from the arrest through the sentencing. The Journal said Wilson "was saved from lynching by the determined attitude of Sheriff La-count," but called him "the negro who assaulted" Mrs. Biggs before any hearing and dwelt on his "surly" manner. Indiana weeklies headed it "Threatened Lynching at Valparaiso" and, in the German-language Indiana Tribüne, "Vor dem Lynchen geschützt."

Elsewhere the wire version ran under headlines such as "INDIANA MOB AFTER BLACK BRUTES" in the Atlanta Constitution. New York papers carried the episode only as the cause of Bowser's movement, and The Sun noted his admitted "deep-rooted antipathy toward the negro race." In September the Dawson News of Georgia reprinted that dispatch under "DON'T WANT THE NEGROES," calling Bowser's fears "not in the least overdrawn."

The local reports place the crowd on Saturday night and describe Sunday as quiet, while the later Laporte dispatches said that "all day Sunday" farmers and college students threatened to break the jail; the local reports are closer to the events. The wire also called the woman "Mrs. Hugh Pitts" or "Bitts" and placed the capture at "Warsaw," and an Iowa brief gave the sentence as fourteen years.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A 'powerful negro' attempted an assault, fled to 'Warsaw', was captured and 'confessed'; angry farmers filled the streets uttering threats, but the jail was not attacked.

accounts.label: Laporte dispatches on Bowser's campaign
accounts.gist: A 'negro tramp' assaulted a farmer's wife; all day Sunday farmers and college or Normal School students clamored to break the jail and lynch him until 'cool men' prevailed.

accounts.label: Wilson's own account
accounts.gist: On arrest he admitted assault and battery but denied rape; at the hearing he pleaded not guilty, and at trial he argued that another Black man committed the act.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal followed the case closely, credited the sheriff for preventing a lynching and reported the departure of Black residents, while calling Wilson 'the negro who assaulted' Mrs. Biggs and dwelling on his 'surly' manner.
The Atlanta Constitution ran the wire under 'INDIANA MOB AFTER BLACK BRUTES' beside Texas mob items; the Bisbee Daily Review headlined 'BURLY NEGRO ATTACKS WIFE OF INDIANA FARMER'.
The Plymouth Tribune headed its account 'Threatened Lynching at Valparaiso' and closed that 'better counsel prevailed'; the Indiana Tribüne headed its item 'Vor dem Lynchen geschützt'.
New York papers carried the episode only as the cause of Bowser's anti-settlement movement, under 'WANTS BLACKS KEPT OUT' and 'WANTS NO MORE NEGROES'.
The Dawson News (Ga.) reprinted the dispatch under 'DON'T WANT THE NEGROES' and said Bowser's fears were 'not in the least overdrawn'.
